content.text: Both domains sit in the same SCOPe 2.08 family, but that family belongs to class k, the designed-proteins class, so the shared family does not carry its usual evolutionary meaning.

answers.answer: No, not in the evolutionary sense. In SCOPe 2.08 both domains are classified in the same family, k.40.1.1 "Designed trimeric coiled-coil" (family sunid 100905; superfamily k.40.1, sunid 100904; fold k.40, sunid 100903). d1s9za_ (sunid 98768, PDB 1s9z chain A) belongs to protein entry "Amyloidogenic design-1" (sunid 103785) and d1hqja_ (sunid 61142, PDB 1hqj chain A) to protein entry "Unnamed design-1" (sunid 100906), both with species "Synthetic". Ordinarily a shared SCOPe family or superfamily is SCOPe's assertion of common ancestry, but this family lies in class k, "Designed proteins" (sunid 58788). Class k is an organizational container for de novo designed, synthetic sequences: its fold/superfamily/family nodes group constructs by design type and architecture (here, engineered trimeric coiled coils), not by inferred descent from a common ancestral protein. These two peptides were designed independently in different laboratories, have no natural ancestor, have no UniProt or Pfam cross-references in SCOPe, and their similarity reflects convergent design to the same heptad-repeat coiled-coil motif. So the correct statement is: same SCOPe class, fold, superfamily and family (k.40.1.1), but this is a shared designed-protein grouping, not evidence of homology; the family-level assignment should not be read as homologous at the usual SCOPe family strength, and function, metal-binding (1s9z with Na/Zn, 1hqj with Pb) or template inferences should not be transferred between them on the basis of this grouping. SCOPe itself attaches no explicit inconsistency or heterogeneity warnings to either domain; the caveat arises from the class k membership.
